title: When the sea route closes
bodyMd:
Roughly four fifths of world merchandise trade by volume moves by sea, and a surprising share of it passes through a handful of narrow places. When traffic through one of those chokepoints is disrupted, a vessel sailing from Asia to northern Europe may be rerouted around the southern tip of Africa, adding some 5,500 kilometres and about ten days to the voyage.

The cost of that detour is not simply extra fuel. A shipping line runs a fixed loop: eight or nine vessels spaced so that one arrives at each port every week. Lengthen the loop by ten days and the same weekly service now needs an extra ship, or two. Because the world's container fleet is close to fully employed in a strong market, the extra ships have to be bid away from other routes, and freight rates rise on routes that were never disrupted at all. That is how a closure in one sea can raise the price of shipping a container between two ports on the other side of the world.

Importers feel the effect with a lag. Goods already afloat arrive late but at the rate contracted before the disruption; goods ordered afterwards carry the new rate, and it is the second batch that reaches the shops. Retailers with short order books therefore absorb the shock later, and more visibly, than the headlines suggest. One further wrinkle rarely makes the front page. Freight is a modest share of the retail price of most manufactured goods, typically low single digits, so even a tripling of container rates moves shelf prices by much less than the rate chart implies. The exceptions are bulky, low-value items, where transport can reach a fifth of the delivered cost, and it is there that a long detour shows up in the price a household actually pays.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage about container shipping and what happens when a sea chokepoint is disrupted. There is no table, figure or mathematical notation. The passage states these figures in words: roughly four fifths of world merchandise trade by volume moves by sea; rerouting a vessel from Asia to northern Europe around the southern tip of Africa adds about 5,500 kilometres and about ten days; a shipping line's weekly loop uses eight or nine vessels; freight is typically a low single-digit percentage of the retail price of manufactured goods; and for bulky, low-value items transport can reach a fifth of the delivered cost.
